question.problem: At which point on the surface $z=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v=⟨4,-2,-1⟩?$
question.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=6x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨4,-2,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩=⟨4,-2,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}6cx=4 \\ 2cy=-2 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
6(1)x=4\,⟹\,x=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
2(1)y=-2\,⟹\,y=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\frac{2}{3}$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+(-1)^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+1 \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(\frac{2}{3},-1,\frac{7}{3}).$
